entries.clue: Fine iced tea brew includes slice of lemon (8)

indicatorNotes.brew: Tea left to brew comes out of the pot changed, and the letters beside the word come out in a changed order too.
indicatorNotes.includes: What includes something makes room for it inside, so the letter named next lands within the jumble rather than beside it.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the drink taken apart
a slice taken off the front of LEMON is its first letter

annotation.surface: An iced tea left to brew with a slice of lemon dropped into the jug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine' sits at the front looking like praise for the tea, which is how a one-word definition hides. Fine here means finely made and easily broken, not excellent.
annotation.definitionFit: Fine → DELICATE: both describe something finely worked and easily damaged, as in fine bone china or a fine thread.

entries.clue: Passionately kiss fashion designer after 1-0? (4)

indicatorNotes.after: 'After' puts the designer's initials second in the queue, so they follow the letters already made rather than leading them.

blocks.note: 1 written out is ONE, the hyphen subtracts and the 0 is the letter O being taken away
CK is the monogram Calvin Klein stitches into everything the label makes

annotation.surface: Someone kissing a fashion designer once the score reaches one-nil.
annotation.walkthrough: '1-0' is a sum rather than a football score: the hyphen takes away and the nought is a letter of the alphabet. Fashion houses are known by their initials, which is how two letters can be a designer.
annotation.definitionFit: Passionately kiss → NECK: to neck is the old slang for a long clinch on the back seat, kissing and cuddling rather than a peck hello.

entries.clue: Heated battle over sea (6)

indicatorNotes.over: In a down clue 'over' is a position rather than a turn: what it names sits higher up the column than what comes next.

blocks.note: a war is fighting on the largest scale, the general word for a battle
the Med is what Britons call the Mediterranean, as in a fortnight in the Med

annotation.surface: A fierce battle being fought out across the Mediterranean.
annotation.walkthrough: Heated and warmed are both past participles, which is what lets one stand in for the other. 'Over' in a down clue is worth banking: it stacks one piece on top of the next.
annotation.definitionFit: Heated → WARMED: both say that heat has been put into a thing, a heated room or a warmed plate straight from the oven.

entries.clue: God admits partners’ stupidity (7)

indicatorNotes.admits: To admit someone is to let them in through the door, so the pair named next finish up inside.

blocks.note: a deity is a god of any religion at all
at the bridge table the players are compass points, and North and South play as a pair

annotation.surface: A god owning up to how foolish his allies have been.
annotation.walkthrough: Bridge supplies the partners: four players named for the compass, bidding two against two. Calling a slow-witted person dense is where the definition comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: stupidity → DENSITY: a dense person is thick-headed, and density is the noun for that thickness of mind as much as for lead.

entries.clue: Frozen without top of thin material (4)

indicatorNotes.without: 'Without' here means going short of something, so the letter it names is dropped rather than added.

blocks.note: glacé is the cook's word for iced or frozen — glacé cherries, glacé icing — and the accent counts for nothing
the top of a word written down the grid is its first letter, and that G goes

annotation.walkthrough: 'Frozen' pulls towards ice and the film, and wants a French cookery word instead. Lace earns 'thin material' because there is more hole than thread in it.
annotation.definitionFit: thin material → LACE: lace is a fine openwork fabric, so little of it solid that you can read through a sheet of it.

entries.clue: 8 queen put on big green pants (6,4)

indicatorNotes.pants: 'Pants' is British slang for rubbish, and a rubbish arrangement of letters is one that has to be sorted out.

blocks.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the cipher stamped on postboxes
eight more letters of fodder, taken straight off the page
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A queen squeezing herself into an enormous pair of green trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a bare number pointing at 8 across, so that clue has to be solved first to know what is wanted. 'Big green' describes nothing here — it is letters.
annotation.definitionFit: 8 → GINGER BEER: 8 across gives the general word for something you drink, and this cloudy, spiced, fizzy one is an example of it.

entries.clue: Prized examples of fruit, large and small (6)

blocks.note: a pear is a fruit, and its four letters come across unchanged
L is the large on a clothing label
S is the small on the same label

annotation.surface: Choice fruit being graded into the large ones and the small ones.
annotation.walkthrough: Garment sizes are a standing convention: S, M, L and XL all arrive as single letters. The definition is plural and figurative, so 'examples' means the things themselves rather than flagging a for-instance.
annotation.definitionFit: Prized examples → PEARLS: a pearl is anything treasured as a perfect specimen of its kind — a pearl of wisdom, a pearl of a performance.

entries.clue: During game First Lady has energy drink (8)

indicatorNotes.During: Whatever happens during a game happens inside it, so the name that follows is planted in the middle of it.

blocks.note: brag is the old British card game of three cards and bluffing that poker grew out of
the first lady of all is the one in Genesis, not a president's wife
E is energy in physics, added on the end

annotation.surface: A president's wife knocking back something energising in the middle of a game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' points hard at the White House and means the garden of Eden. Brag is where setters reach whenever a four-letter game is needed.
annotation.definitionFit: drink → BEVERAGE: beverage is the formal, menu-card word for anything you drink, hot or cold, alcoholic or not.

entries.clue: A story involving Carroll’s lead girl (5)

indicatorNotes.involving: To involve something is to wrap it up in what you are doing, so the letter named next is taken inside.

blocks.note: the clue's own first word, used as itself
a story in the sense a child tells one is a lie
the lead letter of CARROLL

annotation.surface: A tale with Lewis Carroll's leading young heroine in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is the trap: it reads as the leading role and means the first letter of the name in front of it. The surface hands the answer over and the wordplay only confirms it.
annotation.definitionFit: girl → ALICE: a plain girl's name, the one the surface has already put in mind by way of Wonderland.

entries.clue: 100 escape jail ring (4)

indicatorNotes.escape: What escapes is out and gone, so the letter it names is no longer in the word.

blocks.note: the clink is British slang for prison, as in a night in the clink
C is a hundred in Roman numerals, and it is the letter that gets out

annotation.surface: A hundred prisoners breaking out of jail.
annotation.walkthrough: The Clink was a real prison in Southwark, and its name spread to mean any jail. 'Ring' is a noun here, a loop of metal rather than anything a telephone does.
annotation.definitionFit: ring → LINK: one closed loop of a chain is a ring of metal, and a chain is counted in them.

entries.clue: European town beset by germs spread by couriers (10)

indicatorNotes.beset by: To be beset by something is to have it pressing in from every side, so the town finishes up enclosed.
indicatorNotes.spread: Germs spread by getting everywhere they were not, and these letters do the same to their order.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
Essen is a city in the Ruhr, the industrial heartland of Germany

annotation.surface: A continental town overrun by an infection carried from door to door.
annotation.walkthrough: Essen is worth learning: five common letters, a big German city, and a setter's favourite. 'Spread by' reads as one phrase on the surface and splits in two in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: couriers → MESSENGERS: a courier is employed to carry something by hand to a named person, which is the messenger's whole job.

entries.clue: Drunk princess breaks record (6)

indicatorNotes.breaks: What breaks a thing splits it apart, and the princess drops straight into the gap she has made.

blocks.note: a CD is the disc a record comes on
Princess Anne, the late Queen's only daughter

annotation.surface: A tipsy princess smashing a record.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' at the head of a clue nearly always announces an anagram, and here it is the definition instead. The slang sense comes from preserving, like pickled and tanked.
annotation.definitionFit: Drunk → CANNED: slang for the state, from the same sealed-in-a-tin idea that gives pickled, bottled and tanked.

entries.clue: Award – final two exchanged money and the rest gold? (5,5)

indicatorNotes.final two exchanged: Exchanging the final two means the last letter and the one before it swap places, and nothing else moves.

blocks.note: the Nobel is the award, arriving with its last two letters swapped round
M is money, as in the economist's M0 and M1
et al is the Latin 'and the others', the tag at the end of a long list of authors

annotation.surface: An award with its last two placings swapped, offering prize money and gold.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a for-instance: the answer names a whole class of metals that will not corrode, and the clue supplies only its best-known member. The prize is one letter-swap away from a word meaning lofty.
annotation.definitionFit: gold → NOBLE METAL: gold is the standard example of the metals that resist corrosion and never tarnish, so the definition works by example.

entries.clue: God is protecting Earth leading everyone to speculate (8)

indicatorNotes.protecting: To protect a thing is to stand round it and shield it, so what is protected ends up inside.
indicatorNotes.leading: The leading letter of a word is the one at its head, and that single letter is all the word gives up.

blocks.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
E is the standard short form for earth
the head of EVERYONE, one letter joining the end

annotation.surface: A god shielding the planet and taking the whole human race with him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leading' is the pivot: it reads as a god leading people to safety and means the first letter of the word after it. Thor is crosswords' default god whenever four letters are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: speculate → THEORISE: to theorise is to put up an explanation you cannot yet prove, which is what speculating about a cause amounts to.

entries.clue: The Listener’s not half simple, right? (3)

indicatorNotes.not half: Taking a word 'not half' leaves you holding only the front half of it, the back half thrown away.

blocks.note: a simple job is an easy one, and only the front half of EASY is wanted
R is right, as on a map or in a stage direction

annotation.surface: A grumble that whoever is listening is nothing like as simple as they look.
annotation.walkthrough: In British speech 'not half' means the opposite of what it says — 'not half bad' is high praise — so it passes for emphasis while giving an instruction. The capital L makes the definition look like the title of a magazine.
annotation.definitionFit: The Listener → EAR: the ear is the organ that does the listening, so the grand capitalised title is the thing on the side of your head.

entries.clue: Long winded poetry describes flower seen in the mirror (7)

indicatorNotes.describes: To describe a circle is to draw one round something, so the poetry is drawn round the piece named next.
indicatorNotes.seen in the mirror: A word seen in a mirror reads backwards, letter for letter, from its end to its start.

blocks.note: verse is poetry taken as a form
a flower is a thing that flows: the Ob is a river, and it arrives back to front

annotation.surface: A rambling poem about a flower reflected in a mirror.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flower' as one-that-flows is the oldest trick in the British cryptic, and the rivers it hides are short: Ob, Exe, Dee, Po. The Ob runs some 2,000 miles north across Siberia.
annotation.definitionFit: Long winded → VERBOSE: verbose writing or speech uses far more words than the job needs, which is what calling someone long-winded says.

entries.clue: Runner is prepared to tackle 1K (3)

indicatorNotes.prepared: Something prepared has been worked on before use, and these two letters have been turned round in the working.
indicatorNotes.to tackle: To tackle a thing is to get to grips with it, taking hold from both sides at once.

blocks.note: two letters of fodder, hiding in plain sight as a verb
one K means a single letter K, not a thousand of anything

annotation.surface: An athlete getting ready to take on a one-kilometre race.
annotation.walkthrough: '1K' looks like a distance off a race entry form and means one letter. The definition is the smooth strip a sledge or a skater slides along, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: Runner → SKI: a runner is the long smooth strip a sledge or a skate travels on, and a ski is that strip strapped under a boot.

entries.clue: Read about the origin of law throughout sailor’s trials (7)

indicatorNotes.about: Letters sent about the place do not come back in the order they set off in.
indicatorNotes.throughout: What runs throughout a word runs from one end of it to the other, with the outer letters left at either side.

blocks.note: OS is an ordinary seaman, the most junior rating on a ship's books
four letters of fodder
the letter LAW begins with, joining the fodder

annotation.surface: A sailor reading up on where law came from all through his troubles.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pulls 'trials' towards the courtroom and the law book, while the answer wants the other sense, a run of hard experiences. A ship's crew list is full of two-letter ranks.
annotation.definitionFit: trials → ORDEALS: a trial in the sense of a testing experience is an ordeal, the pairing solvers know from 'trials and tribulations'.

entries.clue: Neil cooked oats, maybe to control character (4,4)

indicatorNotes.cooked: Cooking something changes it past recognition, and the name beside the word comes out in a different order.

blocks.note: the four letters of the name, stirred into a new order
oats are one example of animal feed, and 'maybe' is what marks them as an example

annotation.surface: Neil cooking up a pot of porridge to keep a difficult character in check.
annotation.walkthrough: A control character is not a letter at all but a code a keyboard sends, and this one drops the cursor to the next row. Short first names are anagram fodder in disguise.
annotation.definitionFit: control character → LINE FEED: the non-printing code that moves output down one row is a control character, from the days of teleprinters.

entries.clue: Church director installs locks then ran meeting (7)

indicatorNotes.installs: To install something is to fit it into place inside, so the locks are set down in the middle of what went before.

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England, the established church and the default church in a British clue
D is director, as it appears on a film's credits
locks are what a hairdresser cuts

annotation.surface: A church official fitting new locks before running a meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has someone at the door with a screwdriver; the wordplay wants the hair on his head. The definition is a whole phrase, so the answer has to be a past tense.
annotation.definitionFit: ran meeting → CHAIRED: whoever runs a meeting takes the chair, and to chair a meeting is to be the one running it.

entries.clue: Hippies excited to catch fellow swimmer (8)

indicatorNotes.excited: An excited crowd will not stand still in line, and neither will the letters the word governs.
indicatorNotes.to catch: To catch a thing is to close your hands round it, so the letter that follows is trapped inside.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder
F is fellow, the F in the FRS after a scientist's name

annotation.surface: Hippies in a frenzy trying to grab hold of one of their own.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' for a fish is standard crossword shorthand, next to 'flyer' for a bird and 'crawler' for an insect. The creature wanted is a long thin cousin of the seahorse.
annotation.definitionFit: swimmer → PIPEFISH: a fish is a swimmer by trade, and the pipefish is a slender tube-shaped one found in shallow coastal water.

entries.clue: Perhaps cricket side’s exhausted after batting then caught (6)

indicatorNotes.exhausted: A word exhausted has had everything inside it used up, leaving only the letters at each end.
indicatorNotes.after: In a down clue 'after' means further down the column, so this piece follows the one already named.

blocks.note: in cricket the side batting is the side that is in
SIDE with its middle used up leaves the outer pair
ct is how a scorecard records a batsman caught out

annotation.surface: A cricket team worn out after their innings and then caught out.
annotation.walkthrough: Three cricketing senses share one clue: the side that is in, the scorecard's shorthand for a catch, and the game named in the definition — which turns out to be the chirping kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Perhaps cricket → INSECT: 'perhaps' marks a for-instance, and the cricket chirping in the grass is one insect among thousands.

entries.clue: Season starter of nachos – garnish with bit of greenery (6)

indicatorNotes.garnish with: A garnish is set into the dish it decorates, so the letter named first ends up inside the word named next.

blocks.note: a sprig is a small leafy shoot, the parsley laid across the plate
the letter NACHOS starts with, while 'starter' keeps the menu going on the surface

annotation.surface: Nachos to start, finished with a sprig of something green.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Season' at the front reads as an instruction to add salt and pepper, and is a time of year. 'Starter' does two jobs at once, the first course and the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Season → SPRING: spring is one of the four seasons, so the definition names the class and the answer supplies a member of it.

entries.clue: Seal is swimming with gent (6)

indicatorNotes.swimming: Something swimming is loose in the water and free to drift into any position at all.

blocks.note: two letters of fodder, the little verb pulled in whole
four more letters, straight off the page
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A seal out in the water beside a gentleman.
annotation.walkthrough: The seal that swims is the animal; the one wanted is the stamp pressed into hot wax, the kind cut into a ring and worn on the little finger.
annotation.definitionFit: Seal → SIGNET: a signet is the engraved stamp, usually set in a ring, that presses a mark into wax to close and authenticate a letter.

entries.clue: A tip about jewellery making (10)

indicatorNotes.about: Turned about, a word faces the other way and reads from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: the clue's first word, used as itself
in Britain a tip is a rubbish dump, so a tip is a mess — written here back to front
bling is the slang for showy jewellery

annotation.surface: A hint about how jewellery gets made.
annotation.walkthrough: Calling a bedroom a tip is British for calling it a mess, which is the sense needed rather than the gratuity. The wordplay also announces the theme: this grid is strung with jewellery.
annotation.definitionFit: making → ASSEMBLING: assembling a thing is putting its parts together, which is making it in the factory sense, and both words are gerunds.

entries.clue: Group not allowed on the radio (4)

indicatorNotes.on the radio: Something on the radio is heard and never seen, so what counts is the sound of the word rather than its spelling.

blocks.note: a thing not allowed is banned, and said aloud the doubled N is lost

annotation.surface: A group barred from the airwaves.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface tells a censorship story while the definition is the musical sense, so the two readings pull opposite ways. One letter is all that separates the spellings.
annotation.definitionFit: Group → BAND: a band is a group of musicians, and more widely any group acting together, as in a band of brothers.

entries.clue: Hit copper with great force (4)

blocks.note: Cu is copper's symbol in the periodic table
ff is fortissimo on a score, the mark telling a player to play very loudly

annotation.surface: Thumping a policeman as hard as anyone can.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is two-faced in British clues, the metal and the policeman, and the surface wants the one in uniform. A single f on a score is loud, so doubling it is louder still.
annotation.definitionFit: Hit → CUFF: to cuff someone is to strike them with an open hand, the clip round the ear rather than a punch.

entries.clue: Extract 150 over 3.14? (4)

indicatorNotes.over: Turned over, two letters come up the other way round and read from the back.

blocks.note: 150 in Roman numerals is C for a hundred followed by L for fifty
3.14 is pi rounded off, which is what the question mark admits, and it comes out backwards

annotation.surface: A fraction with 150 on top and pi underneath.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' looks like the line of a fraction with one number above the other, and it is a turn instead. The question mark concedes that pi does not stop after two decimals.
annotation.definitionFit: Extract → CLIP: a clip is a short passage cut out of a film or a broadcast and shown on its own.

entries.clue: Mate finally moving to centre of mountain range (5)

indicatorNotes.finally moving to centre: The letter standing last is picked up and set down in the middle, which leaves the word in a new order.

blocks.note: china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, shortened in use to china — my old china
anagram indicator, and a precise one

annotation.surface: A friend edging towards the middle of a mountain range.
annotation.walkthrough: Rhyming slang is the doorway: china plate rhymes with mate, and setters use the shortened half without warning. Moving one named letter rather than jumbling the lot is a rare and exact kind of anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: mountain range → CHAIN: a line of peaks running one into the next is a chain, the word used of the Andes and of any range of hills.

entries.clue: On river long ago, you returned with make-up (8)

indicatorNotes.returned: To return is to come back the way you went, so everything named before the word is read in reverse.

blocks.note: re means on or concerning, as at the head of a memo
the Nile is the river setters reach for when four letters are wanted
ye is the old form of you, and 'long ago' says which century's English to use

annotation.surface: You coming home from a river journey of years ago wearing make-up.
annotation.walkthrough: Three separate pieces go in and the whole string comes back the other way, which is what makes the starting point hard to find. 'Long ago' is a date stamp on the word for you, not a definition.
annotation.definitionFit: make-up → EYELINER: eyeliner is the pencil drawn along the lash line, one cosmetic among many, so the definition works by example.
